title: Common Capabilities — Shared Across Missions
description: Capabilities nearly every public organization relies on, whatever its mission: identity and access, data protection and privacy, records, security logging, and case management, with their reference requirements, example patterns for case management and sign-on, and a short discovery question set. Mission packages build on this one.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
sources.note: Control catalog, including the access control, identification and authentication, audit and accountability, and system and communications protection families.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-4 — Digital Identity Guidelines
sources.note: Requirements for identity proofing, authenticators, and authentication for people who use government systems.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 552a — Records maintained on individuals (Privacy Act of 1974)
sources.note: Limits how agencies disclose records about individuals, with listed exceptions, and requires an accounting of many disclosures.

sources.title: NIST Privacy Framework
sources.note: A voluntary framework for identifying and managing privacy risk, including knowing what personal data is processed and where.

sources.title: 44 U.S.C. § 3101 — Records management by agency heads; general duties
sources.note: Agencies must make and keep records that document their organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, and essential transactions.

sources.title: National Archives — General Records Schedules
sources.note: Approved disposition authorities for records common to many federal agencies.

elements.title: Identity & Access Management
elements.description: Ability to know who is using the office’s systems and to grant, review, and remove their access to information according to their role and need.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Shared across missions. Many offices rely on an agency-wide identity service; the office may still own who gets access to its own systems and records.

elements.title: Data Protection & Privacy
elements.description: Ability to protect sensitive and personal information wherever it’s kept: knowing where it is, limiting who sees it, sharing it only as allowed, and keeping it safe in storage and in transit.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Shared across missions. What counts as sensitive, and which disclosures are allowed, depends on the laws and notices that apply to each office.

elements.title: Records Management
elements.description: Ability to make and keep records of the office’s work and decisions, and to keep or dispose of each kind of record on an approved schedule.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Shared across missions. Schedules for mission-specific records are approved for each agency; the General Records Schedules cover records common to many.

elements.title: Security Logging & Monitoring
elements.description: Ability to record what happens in the office’s systems, such as sign-ins, access to sensitive information, and changes, and to review those records and act on what they show.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Shared across missions. Logging is often run agency-wide; the office decides what in its own systems needs watching.

elements.title: Case Management
elements.description: Ability to track each matter the office handles, such as a request, a complaint, or a case, from the time it arrives until it’s closed: who has it, where it stands, what’s due when, and what belongs to it.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Shared across missions. Each mission adds its own steps, such as triage or review, on top of the same way of tracking work.

elements.title: Grant access by role and need
elements.description: Give each person access to the information and systems their role needs, and no more, and change or remove it when their role changes or they leave.

elements.title: Require strong sign-in
elements.description: Confirm who people are when they sign in, with more than a password for staff and for anything sensitive.

elements.title: Review access regularly
elements.description: Check who has access to what on a regular schedule, and remove access that’s no longer needed.

elements.title: Encrypt sensitive information
elements.description: Protect sensitive information with encryption while it’s stored and while it moves between systems.

elements.title: Know where personal information is kept
elements.description: Keep track of which systems hold personal information, what kinds, and why it was collected.

elements.title: Share personal information only as allowed
elements.description: Disclose records about people only with their consent or under an exception the law allows, and keep an account of disclosures where the law requires one.

elements.title: Keep records of decisions and actions
elements.description: Make and keep records that show how the office is organized and what it decided and did.

elements.title: Keep and dispose of records on approved schedules
elements.description: Keep each kind of record for as long as its approved schedule says, then dispose of it or transfer it as the schedule directs.

elements.title: Record who did what in systems
elements.description: Keep a record of sign-ins, access to sensitive information, and changes, with enough detail to tell who did what and when.

elements.title: Review logs and act on them
elements.description: Look at logged events regularly, by hand or automatically, and follow up on anything unusual.

elements.title: Receive matters through several channels
elements.description: Accept matters, such as requests, complaints, and referrals, through each channel the office offers, like an online form, email, mail, and phone, and record each one in one place.

elements.title: Acknowledge receipt
elements.description: Let the person who sent a matter in know it was received, with a number they can use to ask about it, where that’s possible and appropriate.

elements.title: Show the status of every case in one place
elements.description: Keep each case’s status, assignment, and next steps current and visible to the people who manage the work.

elements.title: Track deadlines
elements.description: Know when each case is due, including deadlines set by law, and warn the people who have it before a deadline passes.

elements.title: Keep a case’s documents with it
elements.description: Keep the documents, correspondence, and notes that belong to a case linked to it, so anyone who picks the case up sees its whole history.

elements.title: Report on the caseload
elements.description: Count cases by type, status, and age whenever they’re needed, for managers and for required reports.

elements.title: Case Management on a Shared Platform
elements.description: An example architecture: case management built on a low-code or CRM platform the agency already runs, with each office getting its own case types, forms, queues, and permissions on the shared foundation.

parts: A case record with status, assignment, due dates, and linked documents, set up for each case type
Intake forms and an email channel that create cases
Work queues and dashboards for each team
Permissions by role that keep one office’s cases apart from another’s
Reports and exports from the same case data
Sign-in through the agency’s identity service, with activity logs sent to agency monitoring
strengths: Uses licenses, skills, and security approvals the agency already has
Offices share one way of tracking work, so reporting across them is easier
New fields and steps can often be added by configuration instead of code
fitsWhen: The agency already runs a platform like this, with people who configure it
The office’s cases are fairly standard, without specialized tools such as redaction or evidence handling
watchFor: Platform administrators can often see every office’s data unless permissions and administration are set up to prevent it
Specialized rules, such as deadlines counted in working days, may need custom work that’s costly to keep up
Upgrades and licensing are decided for the whole agency, not for the office

elements.title: Agency Sign-On with Phishing-Resistant Authentication
elements.description: An example architecture: every system signs staff in through the agency’s identity provider, with phishing-resistant authenticators such as PIV cards or FIDO2 security keys, and grants access through role groups that are reviewed on a schedule.

parts: The agency’s identity provider, with single sign-on to each system
Phishing-resistant authenticators for staff, such as PIV cards or FIDO2 security keys
Role groups that grant access, each owned by the office that owns the system
Steps for people who join, change roles, or leave, tied to personnel actions
Access reviews on a schedule, signed off by system owners
Sign-in and access events sent to security logging
strengths: One strong sign-in for every system instead of a password for each
Removing a person’s access in one place removes it everywhere
Access reviews work from the same groups that grant access
fitsWhen: The agency’s identity provider can connect to the office’s systems
Staff already carry PIV cards or can be issued security keys
watchFor: Systems that can’t use single sign-on keep their own accounts, which need their own reviews
Each role group needs an owner in the office, or access drifts
Members of the public, such as requesters or people who report, need a different way to sign in, or none

elements.title: Collaboration Workspace with Records and Sensitivity Labels
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency’s office suite and collaboration workspace, for documents, chat, and meetings, with retention labels that keep work on approved records schedules and sensitivity labels that limit who can open, share, or copy sensitive information.

parts: Shared documents, chat, and meetings for each team, signed in through the agency
Retention labels that apply an approved records schedule to files and messages
Sensitivity labels that limit opening, sharing, and copying, and protect files that leave the agency
Rules that warn or block when personal or sensitive information is shared outside the team
Search across files and messages for records requests and legal holds
strengths: Records and protection go wherever staff already work, instead of in a separate system
Messages and drafts that are records are kept on schedule, not left to each person
The same labels serve records requests, legal holds, and investigations
fitsWhen: Much of the office’s work happens in documents, email, and chat outside its business applications
Records schedules and sensitivity rules are hard to apply by hand
watchFor: Labels only help if they’re applied, so defaults and automatic labeling matter
Chat and meeting recordings can be records too, which surprises people
Work kept here and in a business application needs one answer to which copy is the record

elements.title: Letters and Notices from Case Data
elements.description: An example architecture: letters, notices, and report sections drafted from approved templates filled in with a case’s data, reviewed and signed by staff, then saved back to the case file.

parts: A library of approved templates, each with an owner
Fields filled in from the case, such as names, dates, and decisions
Review and signature by the responsible person before anything goes out
The sent version saved to the case file, with when and how it was sent
strengths: Required wording, such as appeal rights, is in every letter
Less retyping of what the case already knows
Every letter sent is on the record with its case
fitsWhen: Staff send many similar letters or notices
Letters are written from scratch or copied from old ones today
watchFor: Templates need an owner to keep them current when the law or policy changes
A filled-in letter still needs a person to read it before it goes out

relations.description: Labels and sharing rules protect what’s in the office suite. Information kept in the office’s other systems needs its own protection.
Retention labels keep documents and messages on schedule. Records in case and other business systems need their schedules applied there.
Only the correspondence. The cases themselves are tracked elsewhere.
Staff sign in through the agency, and access follows its role groups.
Fills templates from the case record and saves what’s sent back to it.
